extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in the history and style of American humor, particularly National Lampoon
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and characterizing the distinctive editorial, stylistic, and content principles embodied by National Lampoon magazine (1970–1998). Useful for understanding the magazine's comedic approach and production practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and surrealist content
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine often featured parody and surrealist content. Its issues often had long and short written pieces, a section of actual news items (dubbed 'True Facts'), cartoons, and comic strips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content mix should include parodies of cultural touchstones and surrealist pieces across multiple formats (prose, cartoons, comic strips). The Wikipedia article notes this as a core characteristic rather than a one-off feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting phoniness (no single political stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers joyfully targeted every kind of phoniness, and had no specific political stance (even though individual staff members had strong political views).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should be aimed broadly at hypocrisy and 'phoniness' rather than promoting a consistent political agenda; the magazine attacked various targets across the ideological spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anarchic, boundary‑pushing humor
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine's humor often pushed far beyond the boundaries of what was generally considered appropriate and acceptable. It was especially anarchic, satirically attacking what was considered holy and sacred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable tone for material was deliberately provocative and transgressive. Examples cited include covers and pieces that challenged taboos; this approach is central to the Lampoon identity but also risked controversy and legal/cultural pushback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppressor comedy / superior insider pose
rubrics_metrics.description: P. J. O'Rourke characterized the magazine's comedy: 'What we do is oppressor comedy.... Our kind of comedy says, "I'm O.K.; you're an asshole." We are ruling class. We are the insiders who have chosen to stand in the doorway and criticize the organization. Our comic pose is superior. It says, "I'm better than you and I'm going to destroy you."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedic voice often assumed superiority and aggression toward targets; humor is combative and comes from an 'insider' vantage rather than a defensive/underdog stance. This description acts as a stylistic standard for Lampoon-style material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Themed issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual issues had themes, including topics such as 'The Future', 'Back to School', 'Death', 'Self-Indulgence', and 'Blight'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues are organized around single topics, providing coherence across diverse pieces (editorials, features, cartoons). Thematic curation is part of the magazine's editorial approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorials presented as parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Every regular monthly issue of the magazine had an editorial at the front of the magazine. This often appeared to be straightforward but was always a parody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Front‑of‑issue editorials should mimic the form of a conventional editorial while subverting expectations via parody. The editor role rotated, so the editorial voice could vary between issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Facts: factual-but-ridiculous news briefs
rubrics_metrics.description: 'True Facts' was a section near the front of the magazine that contained true but ridiculous items from real life... essentially a column of funny news briefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain factual basis for the items while emphasizing ludicrousness; this column served as one of the few 'factual' parts of the magazine and was a recurring branded feature with compilation specials and books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foto Funnies / fumetti (photographic comic strips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most issues featured one or more 'Foto Funny' or fumetti, comic strips that use photographs instead of drawings as illustrations. The characters who appeared were usually the male writers, editors, artists, photographers, or contributing editors, often cast alongside nude or semi-nude female models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staged photography and staff participation to create comic narratives; these pieces frequently included sexualized imagery and were a distinctive, recurring feature of the Lampoon format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funny Pages: dedicated comics section
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Funny Pages' was a large section at the back of the magazine that was composed entirely of comic strips of various kinds, including recurring strips and contributions from many artists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve space for serialized and one-off comic strips, showcasing a diversity of cartoonists and styles; this functioned as a magazine-within-a-magazine to concentrate cartoon content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover art: unified, sophisticated, provocative design
rubrics_metrics.description: Michael C. Gross achieved a unified, sophisticated, and integrated look for the magazine, which greatly enhanced its humorous appeal. A number of the Lampoon's most acerbic and humorous covers were designed or overseen by Gross, including provocative gags like the January 1973 'If You Don't Buy This Magazine, We'll Kill This Dog.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art direction should produce a consistent visual identity while using provocative or shocking cover gags that amplify the magazine's comedic stance; considered design elevated the humor and collectible value of issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody of existing media and ads (with legal risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine parodied existing media and advertisements (e.g., a fake Volkswagen Beetle print advertisement); such parodies sometimes led to legal threats and forced removal of material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parodying well-known brands and works is a deliberate tactic but carries risk of trademark or other legal challenges; editors balanced comedic impact against potential legal consequences (example: VW lawsuit over a spoof ad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation of editorial responsibility and staff-driven content
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial role rotated among the staff; different editors or guest editors oversaw issues. Many features (Foto Funnies, True Facts, editorials) involved staff as participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial variability and heavy involvement of the creative staff in content (writing, appearing in photographic pieces, etc.) were structural practices that influenced the magazine's voice and output consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-format, franchise-minded production (print to stage/film/radio)
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine spawned films, radio, live theater, recordings, and print products; many writers and performers used the magazine as a springboard to other media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Lampoon's output or planning work in its spirit, consider translatability of pieces across media (sketches, radio segments, stage shows, films) and the potential for brand/licensing uses—this shaped editorial choices, especially after commercial success like Animal House.
